items.followUp: What is corrosion? State the conditions required for iron to rust.

rubric.why: Rusting is the formation of rust on iron.
rubric.description: Defines rusting as the formation of rust on iron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying rusting as the formation of rust on iron.

rubric.why: Both oxygen and moisture are required for rusting under ordinary conditions.
rubric.description: States that oxygen and moisture are required for rusting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both conditions.

modelAnswer: Rusting is the slow formation of a reddish-brown coating of hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust) on iron.
The important condition for rusting is the presence of both oxygen and moisture.

items.followUp: Why do metals form positive ions in chemical reactions?

rubric.why: Metals characteristically lose electrons and form positively charged ions.
rubric.description: Defines metals by their tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating both the loss of electrons and the formation of positive ions.

modelAnswer: Metals are elements that readily lose electrons to form positively charged ions (cations).

items.followUp: Write two chemical equations that show properties of metals.

rubric.why: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
rubric.description: States that metals react with oxygen to form oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with or without a correct example.

rubric.why: Many metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
rubric.description: States that metals react with acids to form a salt and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with or without a correct example.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides; for example, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas; for example, Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

items.followUp: State Bohr's postulates about electron shells and the emission or absorption of energy.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-orbit or energy-level postulate.

rubric.why: Electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate or lose energy.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate or lose energy in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: An electron absorbs energy when it moves to a higher energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher energy level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing absorption during an upward transition.

rubric.why: An electron emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing emission during a downward transition.

rubric.why: The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between energy levels and is related to radiation frequency by ΔE = hν.
rubric.description: Relates the energy change between levels to the frequency of the radiation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the relation ΔE = hν or its equivalent.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular paths called orbits or shells; each has a definite energy.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
An electron absorbs energy and jumps to a higher energy level when it receives the required energy.
An electron emits energy and jumps to a lower energy level when it loses energy.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the two energy levels and is related to frequency by ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Define a molecule and distinguish between molecules of elements and molecules of compounds, giving examples.

rubric.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest independently existing particle that retains the substance's chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a substantially correct definition.

rubric.why: A molecule of an element contains atoms of the same element, such as O₂, N₂ or H₂.
rubric.description: Identifies molecules of elements and gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and an example.

rubric.why: A molecule of a compound contains atoms of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
rubric.description: States that molecules of compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the constituent atoms and their chemical combination.

rubric.why: H₂O, CO₂ and NH₃ are examples of molecules of compounds.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a molecule of a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain the chemical properties of that substance.
Molecules of elements contain atoms of the same element; for example, O₂.
Molecules of compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; for example, H₂O.
